about: Mastery 1 (CENG40001) is a compulsory 5-credit Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, running across the Autumn and Spring terms. It is the first of three Mastery modules, through which students show their competency in core chemical engineering subjects using a holistic, systems-based approach. No public descriptor gives a fixed syllabus or assessment format, so this is a preparation guide rather than a content pack: check the module's own guidance for the format.

notes.body:
Mastery 1 (CENG40001) is a compulsory 5-credit Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, running across the Autumn and Spring terms. It is the first of three Mastery modules: Mastery 2 (CENG50001) and Mastery 3 (CENG60001) follow in Years 2 and 3, also at 5 credits each.

What the official documents say
- The 2026-27 programme specification states that you study core chemical engineering subjects and demonstrate your competency in them through the "mastery" concept.
- The department describes its approach as holistic and systems-based: problems are analysed and solved as connected wholes rather than topic by topic.
- No public module descriptor sets out a fixed syllabus, the assessment format or the weighting for Mastery 1, so this guide does not invent one.

Assessment: what is and is not confirmed
- The programme specification gives assessment only at programme level. Some assessments in the programme are non-weighted pass/fail elements that you must pass, and the specification says these will be identified at the start of your modules. Check on the module's virtual learning environment page or in the handbook whether any part of Mastery 1 is of this kind.
- To progress from Year 1 you must pass all 60 ECTS of modules (at first attempt, at resit or by compensation), with an overall weighted average of at least 40%. Compulsory modules such as Mastery 1 can be compensated, but no more than 15 ECTS can be compensated over the whole programme.
- Format, timing, permitted materials and pass requirements for Mastery 1 itself should be taken from what the department announces at the start of the module, not from older students' memories, because curricula change.

How to use this pack
Because the content of Mastery 1 is drawn from the core subjects, the best revision is the packs for Process Analysis, Transfer Processes 1, Thermodynamics 1 and Separation Processes 1, plus practice at combining them. The notes that follow explain a systems-based method and give an integrated example. They are preparation for the style of thinking, not a description of a specific paper.

notes.h: How Mastery connects the Year 1 core subjects
notes.body:
The Year 1 core modules listed in the programme specification are Process Analysis, Chemical Engineering Practice 1, Transfer Processes 1, Thermodynamics 1 and Separation Processes 1, alongside compulsory Chemistry 1, Mathematics Fundamentals and Physical Chemistry. The Mastery idea is that competency in this core should be shown on problems that cut across the module boundaries, as a real plant does.

How the subjects naturally link
- Process Analysis provides the bookkeeping: material and energy balances, degrees of freedom, recycle and purge, reaction extents.
- Thermodynamics 1 provides the state of matter: properties, phase behaviour, the first and second laws and enthalpy changes.
- Transfer Processes 1 provides rates: pressure drop and pumping, conduction, convection and diffusion, which decide how big equipment must be.
- Separation Processes 1 combines equilibrium with balances and rates: flash, distillation, absorption and extraction.
- Mathematics underpins all of them: solving linear systems, ordinary differential equations (for example unsteady tank balances) and numerical methods. (A third-party UC Education Abroad Program listing for Chemical Engineering Practice 1, last reviewed 2024-25, says that module introduces MATLAB; the programme specification itself does not name a programming language.)

A typical chain of reasoning
A single plant question can move through several of these in sequence:
1. A mass balance fixes stream flows and compositions.
2. An energy balance fixes a heat duty.
3. A rate equation (Q = UAΔT_lm, or a pressure-drop correlation) turns the duty into an equipment size.
4. Equilibrium data decide how many stages a separator needs.
5. A sanity check (orders of magnitude, units, limiting cases) confirms the answer is physical.

What "systems-based" means in practice
- Draw the boundary first and decide what crosses it.
- Recognise when the overall system is easier to analyse than any single unit (for example, overall balances on recycle loops).
- Track how a change in one unit propagates: a fouled heat exchanger lowers an outlet temperature, which changes a flash split, which changes a recycle flow.
- Distinguish design problems (find the size) from rating problems (equipment is fixed; find its performance).

This is an interpretation of the official description to help you prepare. Use the module's own guidance for the exact scope.

notes.h: Preparing: a systems-based method for problems
notes.body:
Whatever format Mastery 1 takes, the habits below are the core of fluent chemical engineering problem-solving and are worth practising until they are automatic.

A standard method
1. Read and sketch. Draw the flowsheet or equipment with every stream labelled, including the unknowns.
2. Define the system. Mark the boundary you will balance over; try the overall boundary first.
3. Choose a basis and units. Pick a convenient basis and convert everything to consistent SI units.
4. Count degrees of freedom. Unknowns minus independent equations (balances, specifications, equilibrium relations, rate equations). Do not start solving until DOF = 0.
5. State assumptions. Steady state, ideal gas, constant c_p, constant molal overflow, negligible kinetic energy and so on, each with a one-line reason.
6. Solve in a sensible order. Start with equations containing a single unknown; keep symbols until the end where possible.
7. Check. Use an unused balance, check that mole fractions sum to 1, that temperatures and pressures are physical, and that orders of magnitude make sense.
8. Interpret. Say what the number means for the plant and what would change it.

Fundamentals to have at your fingertips (approximate values)
- R = 8.314 J/mol K; g = 9.81 m/s²; 1 atm = 101.325 kPa.
- Water: ρ ≈ 1000 kg/m³, μ ≈ 1 × 10⁻³ Pa s, c_p ≈ 4.18 kJ/kg K, latent heat ≈ 2257 kJ/kg at 100 °C.
- Air: ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ at 20 °C and 1 atm; about 21 mol% O₂.
- Diffusivities: gases ~10⁻⁵ m²/s, liquids ~10⁻⁹ m²/s.
- Pipe flow laminar below Re ≈ 2000.

Common slips that cost marks
- Mixing mass and mole fractions.
- Gauge versus absolute pressure in gas calculations.
- Using kW and kJ/h in the same equation.
- Counting the total material balance as an extra independent equation.
- Forgetting that total moles change in reactions.
- Using the arithmetic instead of the log-mean temperature difference.

How to practise
- Rework past tutorial sheets from the core modules without notes, timing yourself.
- Take a worked problem from one module and extend it with a question from another (for example, size the heat exchanger implied by an energy balance).
- Explain each step aloud: if you cannot say why an equation applies, you have not mastered it.
- Ask the module team what format and resources are allowed, and practise under those conditions.

notes.h: Integrated practice: balances meet heat transfer
notes.body:
This example shows the kind of reasoning that joins Process Analysis, Thermodynamics and Transfer Processes. It is practice material written for this guide, not a past Mastery question.

Problem
2.0 kg/s of water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C in a heat exchanger by saturated steam condensing at 120 °C. Take c_p = 4.18 kJ/kg K for water and a latent heat of 2200 kJ/kg (approximate for steam condensing near 120 °C). The overall heat transfer coefficient is 1500 W/m² K.

Step 1: energy balance on the water
Q = ṁc_pΔT = 2.0 × 4.18 × 50 = 418 kW.

Step 2: steam requirement
The steam gives up its latent heat only (leaving as saturated condensate): ṁ_steam = 418/2200 = 0.19 kg/s.

Step 3: driving force
The steam stays at 120 °C, so the end temperature differences are 120 − 20 = 100 K and 120 − 70 = 50 K.
ΔT_lm = (100 − 50)/ln(100/50) = 72.1 K.
With a condensing fluid at constant temperature, flow arrangement (co- or counter-current) makes no difference.

Step 4: required area (a design problem)
A = Q/(UΔT_lm) = 418 000/(1500 × 72.1) = 3.86 m².

Step 5: what if the exchanger fouls? (a rating problem)
Suppose fouling lowers U to 1000 W/m² K with the same 3.86 m². For a fluid heated by a constant-temperature condensing stream:
ln[(T_s − T_in)/(T_s − T_out)] = UA/(ṁc_p) = 1000 × 3.86/(2.0 × 4180) = 0.462
(T_s − T_out) = 100 × e^(−0.462) = 63 K, so T_out ≈ 57 °C instead of 70 °C.
This links back to the system: a downstream unit expecting 70 °C water now receives 57 °C water, so its own balance changes.

Points the example illustrates
- The energy balance alone gives the duty but not the size; a rate equation is needed for that.
- Physical property values must be stated and labelled as approximate.
- Checking units at each step (kW vs W, kJ vs J) prevents factor-of-1000 errors.
- Design (find A) and rating (find T_out for a given A) use the same equations solved for different unknowns.

Exam tips: in integrated problems, say clearly which principle each step uses (balance, equilibrium or rate) and carry a running list of assumptions.

questions.q: Water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C by steam condensing at 120 °C. What is the log-mean temperature difference?
questions.why: The end differences are 100 K and 50 K, so ΔT_lm = 50/ln 2 = 72.1 K. 75.0 K is the arithmetic mean of the end differences, which overestimates the true mean driving force. 50.0 K is the temperature rise of the water, not a driving force between the two fluids. 100 K is only the inlet-end difference, which overstates the driving force because the gap narrows to 50 K at the outlet.

questions.q: In a non-reactive steady-state problem with three species, a student writes three species balances and the total mass balance and counts four independent equations. What is wrong?
options: Species balances are not valid without reaction, so only the total balance counts
There should be six independent equations, two per species
The total balance is the sum of the species balances, so only three are independent
Nothing: each balance is a separate equation
questions.why: Adding the three species balances gives the total balance, so it adds no new information and there are only three independent equations. Treating all four as independent overstates the equations and gives a wrong DOF. Species balances are perfectly valid without reaction (In = Out for each species). There is one balance per species, not two.

questions.q: 2.0 kg/s of water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C by steam condensing at 120 °C (latent heat 2200 kJ/kg; water c_p = 4.18 kJ/kg K). U = 1500 W/m² K. Find the duty, the steam flow and the heat transfer area.
markScheme: End ΔTs 100 K and 50 K; ΔT_lm = 72.1 K (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Energy balance on the water: Q = ṁc_pΔT = 2.0 × 4.18 × (70 − 20) = 418 kW. The steam condenses at constant temperature giving up latent heat only: ṁ_steam = 418/2200 = 0.19 kg/s. Driving force: ΔT₁ = 120 − 20 = 100 K, ΔT₂ = 120 − 70 = 50 K, so ΔT_lm = 50/ln 2 = 72.1 K. Area: A = 418 000/(1500 × 72.1) = 3.86 m².

questions.q:
A heater uses steam condensing at 120 °C to heat 2.0 kg/s of water from 20 °C to 70 °C (c_p = 4.18 kJ/kg K; latent heat 2200 kJ/kg). The clean overall coefficient is 1500 W/m² K.
(a) Find the duty, steam flow and required area. [8]
(b) After a year, fouling lowers U to 1000 W/m² K. With the same area and water flow, find the new water outlet temperature and steam flow. [8]
(c) Suggest two ways the plant could restore the 70 °C outlet, and comment on their system-level consequences. [4]
markScheme: Rating relation ln[(T_s − T_in)/(T_s − T_out)] = UA/(ṁc_p) used with justification (3 marks)
New duty ≈ 2.0 × 4.18 × 37 ≈ 309 kW; steam ≈ 0.14 kg/s (2 marks)
Two remedies, e.g. raise steam pressure/temperature, clean the exchanger, add area, reduce water flow, with consequences (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Q = 2.0 × 4.18 × 50 = 418 kW. Steam: 418/2200 = 0.19 kg/s. End differences 100 K and 50 K give ΔT_lm = 50/ln 2 = 72.1 K. A = 418 000/(1500 × 72.1) = 3.86 m².

(b) Now the area is fixed and the outlet temperature unknown, a rating problem. For a stream heated by a fluid at constant temperature T_s, a differential balance ṁc_p dT = U(T_s − T)dA integrates to ln[(T_s − T_in)/(T_s − T_out)] = UA/(ṁc_p). With U = 1000 W/m² K: UA/(ṁc_p) = 1000 × 3.86/(2.0 × 4180) = 0.462. So T_s − T_out = 100 × e^(−0.462) = 63.0 K and T_out = 57.0 °C. (Check for the clean case: 1500 × 3.86/8360 = 0.693 = ln 2, giving T_out = 70 °C.) New duty = 2.0 × 4.18 × (57.0 − 20) = 309 kW, so steam falls to 309/2200 = 0.14 kg/s (taking the same latent heat).

(c) Options: (i) raise the steam pressure so it condenses at a higher temperature, increasing ΔT_lm; this needs higher-pressure steam (more expensive, and the exchanger shell must be rated for it), and fouling may accelerate at higher wall temperature. (ii) Clean the exchanger to restore U; this needs a shutdown or a spare exchanger. (iii) Add area (a second shell) to allow for fouling in design. (iv) Reduce the water flow; the outlet then reaches a higher temperature, but downstream throughput falls. Each choice changes something else in the system, such as the steam balance on the site, the downstream unit's feed rate, or capital cost, which is the point of a systems view.
